record.paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
record.original_question: If RIS elements cannot be perfectly deactivated in practice, how does imperfect deactivation change the accuracy and robustness of channel-estimation methods that assume complete absorption, complete transmission, or complete removal of RIS reflections?

evidence.quote: Also, analyzing the effect of imperfect deactivation on the accuracy of estimation methods is an important future direction for research.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication system equipped with a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) consisting of N passive reflecting elements. Let the cascaded channel between a single-antenna transmitter and a single-antenna receiver via the RIS be modeled as

 y = (h_d + g^T diag(theta) f) x + n,

where h_d ∈ C is the direct (non-RIS) channel, f ∈ C^N is the transmitter-to-RIS channel, g ∈ C^N is the RIS-to-receiver channel, x is the transmitted pilot, n ~ CN(0, sigma^2) is additive Gaussian noise, and theta = (theta_1, ..., theta_N)^T ∈ C^N collects the reflection coefficients of the RIS elements. In an ideal model, each element n can be configured in one of three "deactivated" modes:
 (i) complete absorption: theta_n = 0,
 (ii) complete transmission (pass-through): the element forwards x with unit gain and no phase shift to the receiver via the direct path,
 (iii) complete removal of reflection: the element contributes nothing to g^T diag(theta) f.

Many channel-estimation schemes for f and g (or for the cascaded coefficients g_n f_n) rely on switching subsets of RIS elements into one of these idealized deactivated states during pilot transmissions in order to isolate or cancel contributions. In practice, however, an element configured to be "deactivated" still produces a residual reflection coefficient theta_n^res, which can be modeled as a random variable on C with |theta_n^res| ≤ epsilon for some leakage parameter epsilon > 0 (or, more generally, with a specified distribution centered near 0 but with nonzero mean and variance).

Problem. Develop a quantitative analysis of how this imperfect deactivation affects channel estimation of (h_d, f, g). Specifically:

(a) For a given estimator E (e.g., least squares, LMMSE, or compressed-sensing-based) that assumes ideal deactivation, derive the bias and mean-square error of the resulting estimates of h_d, f, and g as functions of the leakage statistics of {theta_n^res} and of N.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the leakage distribution (in terms of epsilon, mean, and covariance) under which the estimator E remains consistent as the pilot length and/or N tend to infinity.

(c) Design channel-estimation procedures that are provably robust to imperfect deactivation, in the sense that their worst-case MSE over all leakage distributions satisfying the assumed constraints is minimized, and characterize the optimal estimator and the corresponding fundamental performance limits (e.g., a Cramér–Rao-type bound) in the presence of imperfect deactivation.
artifact.status_search_result: The question of quantifying and mitigating the effect of imperfect deactivation of RIS elements on channel-estimation methods is explicitly identified as an open research direction in the RIS channel-estimation literature. A web check did not surface a paper that provides a complete analytical answer (bias/MSE characterization, consistency conditions, and robust-optimal estimators) for this specific problem.
